passage: I have never been a jealous man. I mention only for completeness that I had by then read her correspondence twice, and that I knew the arrival times of every train from the north.
question: The second sentence invites the reader to conclude that:
choices: the narrator's denial is contradicted by the conduct he reports as incidental
the narrator was conducting a legitimate inquiry into a genuine concern
the narrator has an unusually precise memory for schedules and details
the narrator is being falsely accused of jealousy by other characters

passage: Everyone at the firm agreed I had been treated unfairly. I could see it in how they went quiet when I came into the room, and in the fact that not one of them would say it to my face.
question: The evidence the narrator offers actually suggests:
choices: the colleagues' behavior admits a reading opposite to the one he draws
the colleagues were intimidated by the seniority of his position
the firm had instructed the staff not to discuss the matter openly
the narrator was indeed treated unfairly and the staff knew it

passage: My sister remembers our childhood as difficult. She was very young, of course, and she has always been sensitive, and she was not there for the worst of it, having been sent to our aunt's for those two years.
question: The final clause undermines the narrator by:
choices: giving a reason her account might be limited that also explains why it might be worse
showing that the sister has confused her own childhood with the narrator's
confirming that the narrator experienced hardships the sister was spared
establishing that the aunt was the source of the sister's false memories

passage: The accident was nobody's fault. The road was wet, the corner is a bad one, and I had had, at most, two glasses, or possibly three, though I had eaten a substantial lunch.
question: The narrator's self-correction chiefly functions to:
choices: expose the anxiety behind an account he is presenting as untroubled
clarify a genuine uncertainty about the events of that afternoon
demonstrate his commitment to reporting the facts with precision
shift responsibility onto the condition of the road at the corner

passage: She left because she wanted a different sort of life. That is what she said in the note, and I have the note still, and I have read it many times, and it says nothing at all about me.
question: The final clause suggests that the narrator:
choices: is reading the note for an absolution or accusation it does not contain
has correctly established that her departure had nothing to do with him
has lost the portion of the note in which she explained her reasons
believes that she wrote the note in haste and without much thought

passage: I gave the boy every opportunity. I paid for the school, I found him the position, I introduced him to the men who mattered, and I asked nothing of him in return but that he should be the sort of person I could mention.
question: The final clause reveals that the narrator's generosity was:
choices: conditional on a return he does not recognize himself as having demanded
entirely selfless and misunderstood by the boy who received it
motivated by a debt he owed to the boy's family from before
insufficient, since he never offered the boy any real affection

passage: The village was welcoming. Within a month I knew everybody's business, and they knew mine, and there was nothing at all that could be done about that, and I do not think about it now more than once or twice a day.
question: The final clause indicates that the narrator:
choices: is preoccupied by an intrusion the account has just described as welcome
has successfully put an unpleasant period of his life behind him
found the village's curiosity a minor and quickly forgotten irritation
is reporting the frequency of his thoughts with careful accuracy

passage: I was, I think, a good father. The children were fed and clothed and never once went without. I could not tell you now what either of them wanted to be, but then I do not think they ever told me.
question: The last sentence functions to:
choices: supply the omission that quietly refutes the standard he has set
confirm that the children were secretive and withheld their plans
show that the narrator's memory has faded with the passing years
establish that the children's ambitions changed too often to track

passage: Naturally I forgave her at once. I have never mentioned it since, except of course on the occasions when it was relevant, and it has been relevant more often than either of us expected.
question: The qualification reveals the forgiveness to be:
choices: retained as a resource rather than actually given up
genuine but tested by unusually frequent circumstance
a formality that neither party had believed in at all
conditional on her never repeating the original offence

passage: The doctor said there was nothing wrong with me that a holiday would not cure. He said it kindly. He said it three times, in three appointments, over five months, and on the last occasion he wrote something down and did not show me.
question: The final detail suggests that:
choices: the reassurance the narrator reports may not be what the doctor believed
the doctor was negligent in failing to arrange any proper tests
the narrator was correct that a holiday was all that he required
the doctor had grown impatient with a patient who would not listen

passage: We parted on good terms. I say this with confidence because I have written to him every Christmas for nine years, and a man does not do that where there is bad feeling.
question: The narrator's reasoning is undermined by the fact that he:
choices: offers his own persistence as evidence of a mutual state he cannot know
has continued a correspondence that plainly caused him some distress
should have written more frequently than once in each calendar year
chose Christmas, which is a season when such letters are conventional

passage: It is quite untrue that I was ever asked to leave. The arrangement had run its natural course, and both parties recognized this, and the letter I received merely set out in writing what had already been settled between us in a conversation I do not now recall.
question: The final clause damages the denial by:
choices: conceding that he cannot vouch for the agreement he is relying on
revealing that the letter had been sent to the wrong recipient
showing that the arrangement had lasted longer than was intended
admitting that the other party had a different account of events

passage: My wife will tell you I am difficult. She will tell you this in a particular voice, with her head slightly turned, and people will laugh, and I will laugh, and later in the car neither of us will say anything for some time.
question: The detail about the car reveals that:
choices: the shared joke covers an injury that both of them register privately
the narrator is exhausted after an evening of unwelcome socializing
the wife's accusation is accurate and the narrator has conceded it
the couple have nothing further to discuss after a pleasant evening

passage: The surgeon emerged after eleven hours, sat down beside them, and said that it had not been entirely straightforward.
question: The surgeon's phrasing is best understood as:
choices: a deliberate minimizing that signals the gravity it declines to state
an accurate and neutral summary of a procedure of moderate difficulty
an attempt to conceal from the family that an error had been made
an indication that the surgeon was too exhausted to explain properly

passage: The expedition's log for the fourteenth reads, in full: "Lost the tents. Weather freshening. Shall not write much tomorrow."
question: The final sentence conveys:
choices: an expectation of disaster stated in the language of minor inconvenience
an intention to conserve paper for the remainder of the journey
a plan to travel too far the next day to permit any writing
a straightforward account of the day's uneventful proceedings

passage: "How was it?" they asked, when he came back from the war. He said the food had been poor, and asked if there was any tea.
question: His answer functions to:
choices: close off a subject whose weight the triviality is chosen to indicate
report accurately the aspect of the war he had found most trying
reassure his family that the experience had not been a difficult one
indicate that he had been kept far from any actual fighting

passage: The company's annual report noted that the fire had presented certain operational challenges, and that the affected site would not be returning to service.
question: The second clause works because it:
choices: states the total loss in language that keeps the first clause's calm
corrects the impression of severity created by the first clause
reveals that the company intends to relocate its main operations
concedes that the challenges had proved more costly than expected

passage: She had, the obituary said, a long association with the hospital. It did not say that she had founded it, or that she had mortgaged her house twice to keep it open.
question: The contrast between the two sentences chiefly demonstrates:
choices: how thoroughly a formula can bury the substance of a life
that the obituary's author had not researched her adequately
that she had preferred her contributions to remain unmentioned
that the hospital had failed to acknowledge its own founder

passage: "I think we may have a small problem with the hull," said the engineer, who was by then standing in water up to his knees.
question: The comedy of the line depends on:
choices: the gap between the engineer's phrasing and the situation described
the engineer's failure to understand how serious the leak was
the reader's uncertainty about whether the ship would in fact sink
the engineer addressing a person who could not do anything about it

passage: He was not a man much given to displays of feeling. When the telegram came he read it, put it in his pocket, went out to the field, and did not come back until it was too dark to see.
question: The final clause conveys:
choices: a grief expressed entirely through the length of an ordinary absence
a determination to complete the day's work despite the interruption
an indifference to the news that the telegram had brought him
a wish to avoid the other members of the household that evening

passage: The review, in its entirety, read: "The soup arrived warm. Of the remaining eleven courses, the less said the better. Parking is available."
question: The middle sentence achieves its effect by:
choices: refusing to describe a failure in terms that imply it beggars description
conceding that the reviewer had not sampled the remaining courses
indicating that the courses were merely unremarkable rather than bad
suggesting that the restaurant had asked for the review to be softened

passage: Asked at the inquiry whether he had considered the risk, the director replied that the matter had been raised, and that a note had been made of it.
question: The reply is damaging because it:
choices: describes a response so minimal that it amounts to having done nothing
admits that the director had personally overlooked the risk entirely
shows that the director was unable to recall the events accurately
reveals that the note had been destroyed before the inquiry began

passage: My father's entire commentary on the four years he spent in the camp was that he had learned to sleep anywhere, which he offered once, as advice, when I complained about a hotel.
question: The passage's force comes from:
choices: an enormity compressed into a remark offered as a household tip
the father's inability to recall the details of his imprisonment
the narrator's failure to ask his father any further questions
the contrast between the hotel's comfort and the camp's conditions

passage: It is fair to say the merger did not achieve everything its architects had hoped. Of the two companies involved, neither now exists.
question: The second sentence functions to:
choices: deliver the scale of the failure while sustaining the measured tone
correct the first sentence, which had overstated the difficulties
explain the particular mechanism by which the merger went wrong
indicate that the architects of the merger had been dismissed

passage: "Bit of a turnout," said the sergeant, looking down the hill at what the whole of the county appeared to have sent.
question: The remark's effect relies on:
choices: a diminishing phrase set against a scale the sentence then supplies
the sergeant's inability to estimate large crowds with any accuracy
the reader's knowledge that the county was sparsely populated
the sergeant's disappointment at how few people had actually come

passage: The letter closed: "We regret that your position has been affected by the reorganization. We should be glad to have the key by Friday."
question: The second sentence intensifies the first by:
choices: following a euphemism with a practical demand that removes all doubt
apologizing a second time for the inconvenience being caused
offering the recipient a reasonable period in which to prepare
implying that the recipient might be permitted to return later
